title: Choosing Without Order
coreInsight: Combinations arise by counting ordered selections and then removing the artificial order that does not matter to the outcome.
targetLearnerRealization: Choosing r objects without order can be derived from ordered selections by dividing out the r! orderings of each group.
learningObjectives: Define what makes two selections the same outcome before counting.
Derive a combination count from ordered selections by proving that each group has r! orderings.
Use combination counts inside multi-stage counting problems without relying on keywords.

continuity.openingCallback: Briefly recall that ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, and CBA are six descriptions of one role-free triple, then enlarge the roster.
closingSeeds: A path can be described by choosing which step positions are, for example, the rightward steps.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Permutation-versus-combination problems can be solved by keyword matching.
It is unnecessary to define what counts as the same outcome.
n choose r is a formula with no relation to ordered counting.

beats.purpose: Briefly reactivate the six ordered descriptions of one fixed triple before advancing to a new choose-three count.
beats.expectedRealization: ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, and CBA are six lineup descriptions of one role-free group.
beats.transitionIn: Remember the six lineups ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, and CBA?
beats.transitionOut: One role-free triple can hide behind six ordered descriptions. Now enlarge the roster.
beats.prompt: As lineups they differ, but as a role-free group they all contain exactly {A, B, C}.

visual.ariaLabel: Six ordered lineups grouped as descriptions of the same three-person group

beats.takeaway: One chosen triple has 3! = 6 ordered descriptions.

beats.purpose: Advance immediately to choosing three from five and derive the unordered count from ordered selections and six-description bundles.
beats.expectedRealization: The 60 ordered three-person descriptions form 10 equal bundles of 3! descriptions, one bundle per role-free group.
beats.transitionIn: Five people—A, B, C, D, and E—are available, and a group needs three people with no roles.
beats.transitionOut: The count came from ordered selections, but the answer counts equal bundles of descriptions that name the same group.
beats.prompt: How many different role-free groups of three can be chosen from the five people?

visual.ariaLabel: Five available people with a prompt to choose a role-free group of three

response.feedback: Count ordered choices first, then use the six lineups of each fixed triple.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct—the 60 ordered descriptions form 10 groups of six.
beats.incorrectFeedback: There are 5×4×3 ordered descriptions. Each role-free group appears in all 3! orders.

visual.ariaLabel: Sixty ordered descriptions divided into bundles of six to make ten role-free groups

steps.title: Count ordered descriptions
steps.body: Choose a first, second, and third listed person from five distinct people.

steps.title: Find one bundle size
steps.body: Each fixed group of three has 3 × 2 × 1 = 3! = 6 name orders, and all six describe the same group.

steps.title: Count the groups
steps.body: Every ordered description belongs to the one group containing those same three people, so the 60 descriptions split into equal bundles of six.

resolution.takeaway: Count ordered selections, then divide by the 3! descriptions of each role-free triple.

beats.purpose: Establish that grouping ordered selections by their underlying set covers the numerator exactly once and creates non-overlapping equal bundles.
beats.expectedRealization: Every ordered selection belongs to exactly one unordered group, so equal r!-sized bundles cover the ordered count without overlap.
beats.transitionIn: The calculation used bundles of six. Division also needs every ordered description to land in exactly one bundle.
beats.transitionOut: Coverage, non-overlap, and equal bundle size turn the division into a complete counting argument.
beats.prompt: Why do the bundles count every unordered group exactly once? Select both required facts.

options.text: Every ordered selection has one underlying set of chosen objects.
An ordered selection cannot belong to two different underlying sets.
Every ordered selection is written alphabetically.

response.feedback: Check that no ordered description is missed and none is placed into two true-outcome bundles.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—every description lands in one and only one group bundle.
beats.incorrectFeedback: You need one fact preventing gaps and another preventing overlap.

steps.title: Coverage
steps.body: Ignoring order in any ordered selection leaves one underlying chosen set, so every description enters a bundle.

steps.title: Non-overlap
steps.body: The same ordered list cannot contain two different sets of objects, so it enters only one bundle.

steps.title: Equal size
steps.body: If r distinct objects are chosen, each bundle contains all r! orders of those same objects.

resolution.takeaway: The ordered selections are partitioned into complete, non-overlapping bundles of size r!.

beats.purpose: Introduce combination language and notation only after the learner has constructed the quotient from equal order bundles.
beats.expectedRealization: C(n,r) names the unordered count obtained by dividing the ordered selection count by r!.
beats.transitionIn: You now have a repeatable operation: count ordered selections, partition them by underlying group, and count the bundles.
beats.transitionOut: Use the notation as a compact record of that argument, not as a keyword-triggered formula.
beats.name: Combinations: choosing without order
beats.conciseDefinition: A combination is a selection in which rearranging the chosen objects does not create a new outcome.
beats.formalization: C(n,r) = n choose r = n(n−1)···(n−r+1) ÷ r! = n!/[r!(n−r)!]
beats.memoryHook: Count ordered picks; divide out the orders of the chosen r.

beats.purpose: Apply the newly derived combination count to the approved authentic starters problem and contrast it with a valid complement shortcut.
beats.expectedRealization: The 24 ordered three-player lineups form four complete bundles of 3! orders, so there are four starter groups.
beats.transitionIn: Now the roster grows to four while the chosen group has size three. Decide first whether lineup order changes the starter team.
beats.transitionOut: The combination derivation gives 24÷6=4; choosing the one person who sits out independently confirms the same four teams.
beats.whyNow: Choosing three starters from four people is a nearly pure combinations application immediately after the learner has proved why a three-person group's six orders are duplicates.
beats.entryBridge: Count 4×3×2 lineups, then group together lineups containing the same three names.
beats.exitBridge: The four bundles can also be labeled by who sits out, providing an independent check without replacing the combination derivation.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Group cards with the six ordered lineups of each three-person set nested underneath.
learnerPrompts: Four players are available. What single choice could determine the other three starters?
Why is choosing 1 player to sit out equivalent to choosing 3 starters?
How does each bench case produce one distinct starter team?
Why are there exactly 4 choices for who sits out?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Count ordered lineups first, then divide by all 3! orders of each same starter group.

visual.ariaLabel: Twenty-four ordered starter lineups grouped into four teams of three, six lineups per team

steps.title: Count ordered lineups
steps.body: Choose a first, second, and third listed player from the four-person roster.

steps.title: Prove the bundle size
steps.body: Each fixed starter group contains three distinct people, so its names have 3! = 6 orders. All six mean the same starter team.

steps.title: Count the bundles
steps.body: The 24 lineups partition into non-overlapping bundles of six.

steps.title: Another way: change what we count
steps.body: Instead of choosing the 3 starters, choose the 1 player who sits out. There are 4 choices.

resolution.takeaway: The combination derivation is the main method here. The sit-out view confirms the answer and shows how changing what we count can make the same problem easier.

beats.purpose: Directly break keyword matching by holding the verb choose constant while changing whether roles distinguish outcomes.
beats.expectedRealization: The outcome definition—not the word choose—determines whether order is artificial.
beats.transitionIn: The word choose appears in all four situations. For each one, decide what swapping the two selected people would do to one complete outcome.
beats.prompt: Sort each situation by whether swapping the two chosen people creates a new outcome.

items.text: choose two starters with equal roles
choose a gold and silver medalist

response.feedback: Name one full outcome, swap the people, and ask whether the roles or result changed.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—the same verb can describe ordered roles or an unordered group.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Ignore the word choose. Test whether swapping the selected people changes the roles or result.

cases.label: Swapping gives the same outcome
items: choose two starters with equal roles

cases.label: Swapping gives a different outcome
items: choose a gold and silver medalist

visual.ariaLabel: Completed classification showing which choosing situations change when the selected people are swapped

steps.body: A committee or equal-role starter pair is unchanged by swapping its written order, so divide away that artificial order.
President/treasurer and gold/silver assign different roles, so swapping people creates a genuinely different outcome.

resolution.takeaway: There is no reliable combination keyword. Define sameness first.

beats.purpose: Set an outcome-first routine for independent practice.
beats.expectedRealization: Each calculation should identify the outcome, ordered numerator, and justified divisor.
beats.transitionIn: Now use the method without being told whether each situation is a combination.
beats.heading: For each problem, say what one outcome is
beats.body: Then count an ordered version if useful. Divide by r! only when all r! orders of the chosen objects describe that same outcome.
math: ordered selections ÷ orders per true outcome = true outcomes
beats.transitionOut: Start with two pure selections, then handle problems where roles or extra stages change the count.

beats.purpose: Provide independent near transfer to a choose-three setting with no roles.
beats.expectedRealization: Choosing three of six distinct posters gives 6×5×4÷3! = 20 displays.
beats.whyNow: The group size stays three while the roster expands, requiring the same verified 3! correction without the starter context.
beats.entryBridge: One display is a set of posters; their order of selection is not displayed.
beats.exitBridge: The ordered count of 120 descriptions forms bundles of six, giving 20 displays.
learnerPrompts: How many ordered descriptions does each display have?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—20 sets of three posters are possible.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Count 6×5×4 ordered selections, then divide by the 3! orders of each fixed set.

steps.title: Count ordered selections
steps.body: Fill three selection positions with distinct posters.

steps.title: Remove order
steps.body: Each displayed set of three appears in all 3! = 6 selection orders.

resolution.takeaway: C(6,3) = 20 because every set has exactly six ordered descriptions.

beats.purpose: Provide independent near transfer to choose-two while requiring the learner to define one mutual connection as the outcome.
beats.expectedRealization: Each handshake pair has two ordered person-to-person descriptions, so C(7,2)=21.
beats.whyNow: Returning to pairs checks that the learner chooses the divisor from the group size rather than carrying over 3! mechanically.
beats.entryBridge: This time r=2. Recompute the multiplicity instead of reusing the previous divisor.
beats.exitBridge: The 42 directed descriptions pair by reversal, producing 21 handshakes.
learnerPrompts: Does Kai-to-Mina differ from Mina-to-Kai as one handshake?
What is r for this selection?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Count 7×6 directed descriptions and bundle each with its reversal.

steps.body: Seven choices for one named endpoint and six for the other give 42 directed descriptions.
A handshake has two people and no direction, so each appears in 2! orders.

resolution.takeaway: The divisor is r!, determined by the number r chosen—not by the previous example.

beats.purpose: Mix an unordered team selection with a genuinely ordered assignment of two different offices.
beats.expectedRealization: Choose the four-person team without order, then assign chair and recorder as distinct roles.
beats.whyNow: The problem uses the word choose for both a role-free group and distinct offices, directly testing outcome definitions rather than keyword matching.
beats.entryBridge: Separate the choice that ignores order from the later choice where the two offices are different.
beats.exitBridge: Fifteen possible teams each support twelve chair-recorder assignments, for 180 outcomes.
learnerPrompts: Which stage is unchanged when names are rearranged?
Does swapping the chair and recorder keep the same outcome?
beats.incorrectFeedback: First choose the four-person team. Within that fixed team, count ordered chair-recorder assignments.

steps.title: Choose the team
steps.body: Order does not distinguish the four volunteers, so choose 4 from 6.

steps.title: Assign distinct offices
steps.body: For each team, there are 4 choices for chair and then 3 for recorder.

steps.title: Combine the stages
steps.body: Every team can be paired with every valid officer assignment.

resolution.takeaway: Use combinations only for the stage where rearranging the selected people changes nothing.

beats.purpose: Connect combinations back to ordered arrangements by decomposing an ordered code into choose-then-arrange stages.
beats.expectedRealization: Choosing three symbols and then ordering them multiplies C(8,3) by 3!, recovering the ordered count 8×7×6.
beats.whyNow: The reverse construction makes the relationship between combinations and permutations explicit and blocks treating them as unrelated formulas.
beats.entryBridge: Here the final positions matter. You may count directly, or choose the symbols first and restore their orders.
beats.exitBridge: The factors cancel conceptually: removing 3! orders creates groups, and restoring 3! orders creates codes.
learnerPrompts: If the three symbols are already chosen, how many codes can they form?
Why should a direct ordered count agree?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Choose 3 of the 8 symbols, then arrange each chosen set in 3! orders.

steps.title: Choose the symbols
steps.body: Ignoring positions for the moment gives C(8,3) sets.

steps.title: Restore meaningful order
steps.body: Each set of three distinct symbols forms 3! = 6 different codes.

steps.title: Check directly
steps.body: Filling the three code positions directly gives the same result.

resolution.takeaway: Combinations remove artificial order; multiplying by r! restores order when positions genuinely matter.

beats.purpose: Use the approved buffet problem to combine a choose-two factor with two independent ordinary choices.
beats.expectedRealization: The vegetable stage contributes C(4,2)=6, which multiplies by 3 meat and 4 dessert choices to give 72 meals.
beats.transitionIn: One final problem hides an unordered selection inside a longer product. Treat each stage according to what one meal records.
beats.transitionOut: The meal count succeeds because the combination factor corrects only the vegetable stage; meat and dessert remain ordinary independent choices.
beats.whyNow: The authentic problem requires the learner to embed an unordered choose-two count inside the product rule after pure combination practice.
beats.entryBridge: Count meat and dessert choices first, then inspect whether corn-potatoes and potatoes-corn are different vegetable selections.
beats.exitBridge: Three meats, four desserts, and six unordered vegetable pairs multiply to 72 meals.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Ordered vegetable-pick descriptions collapsing into unordered pair cards.
learnerPrompts: At the first step, why do the 3 meat choices and 4 dessert choices make 12 pairs?
At the ordered-pick trap, which reversed vegetable descriptions name the same pair?
When the six pair cards appear, how do they show C(4,2)?
At the final step, why do the three independent factors multiply?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Keep your answer while you step through the stages. Check whether your vegetable factor counts each pair once or twice.

steps.title: Choose meat and dessert
steps.body: These are independent single choices.

steps.title: Correct the vegetable count
steps.body: Four choices then three choices gives 12 ordered descriptions, but every pair appears in two orders.

steps.title: Build a complete meal
steps.body: Every meat-dessert pair can be combined with every unordered vegetable pair.

resolution.takeaway: In a multi-stage count, use a combination exactly where order is artificial, then multiply the independent stage counts.

beats.purpose: Consolidate the complete reasoning chain before the forward hook.
beats.expectedRealization: A combination argument defines sameness, counts ordered selections, proves complete non-overlapping r!-sized bundles, and then divides.
beats.transitionIn: Across teams, handshakes, codes, and meals, the notation changed less than the meaning of one outcome did.
beats.prompt: Which checks justify dividing an ordered selection count by r!? Select all four.

options.text: Reordering the r chosen objects does not change the true outcome.
Every true outcome has all r! orders as descriptions.
Every ordered selection belongs to some true-outcome bundle.
No ordered selection belongs to two different bundles.
The problem uses a word such as team or choose.

response.feedback: A word cannot justify division. Look for sameness, equal multiplicity, coverage, and non-overlap.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes—that is a complete combination argument, not a formula guess.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Check what makes outcomes the same and why the ordered descriptions partition into equal bundles.

visual.ariaLabel: Four-stage checklist for deriving a combination count

steps.body: For n available objects and r chosen objects, the ordered numerator is n(n−1)···(n−r+1).
If order is artificial, each true group has exactly r! descriptions, and the bundles partition the numerator.

resolution.takeaway: Choose notation compresses a partition argument: ordered descriptions grouped into equal r!-sized bundles.

beats.purpose: Create a concrete successor question linking path strings to choosing positions, without beginning the grid-path lesson.
beats.expectedRealization: A path with fixed step counts may be encoded by choosing which positions contain one type of step.
beats.transitionIn: One more setting hides a choice-without-order inside an ordered-looking object.
beats.prompt: A shortest grid path uses three R steps and two U steps. If its five step positions are numbered, could the whole path be determined just by choosing the three positions that contain R?
beats.takeaway: Choosing positions may count paths. Next, that viewpoint will connect combinations to grid paths and Pascal's Triangle.

notes: Draft foundation lesson authored with the repo-local mathinking-lesson Skill.
The opening moves from the six orders of one fixed triple to choosing three of five: 60 ordered descriptions divided into 10 equal bundles of 3! descriptions.
The authentic starters problem uses a static bundle visualization for the primary 24÷6 derivation, followed by its existing complement animation as an elegant alternate viewpoint.
The authentic buffet animation is integrated as controlled four-step transfer.
All visuals reuse existing generic primitives; no lesson-specific renderer behavior was added.
